excerpt: In a review and meta-analysis commissioned by the U.S. Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, mindfulness-based interventions compared to active controls had only moderate efficacy for anxiety, depression, and pain; low efficacy for stress and quality of life; and no effect or insufficient evidence for attention, positive mood, substance abuse, eating habits, sleep, and weight control.
overview: This evidence item qualifies popular therapeutic claims by separating domains with moderate evidence from domains with weak or absent evidence. It supports a condition-specific interpretation: mindfulness interventions may be useful in some contexts, but the source rejects broad claims of strong or universal clinical efficacy.
title: Mixed Active-Control Efficacy
